newsitem.title: GERMANY: Kohl asks Germans to meet new economic challenges.
newsitem.headline: Kohl asks Germans to meet new economic challenges.

text.p: Chancellor Helmut Kohl, in a New Year's message, on Tuesday called on Germans to accept cuts in the comprehensive welfare system and meet new economic challenges if they wanted to maintain prosperity.

The need to slash spending and reform restrictive economic and labour practices has become a perennial theme in the last two years as Germany has struggled to overcome stagnant growth and record unemployment, to fulfil the criteria for EMU.

The text of Kohl's televised New Year address, released in advance on Monday, indicated this was not about to change in 1997, as competition got even tougher and the assumptions that governed decades of post-war prosperity were no longer valid.
"The globalisation of the economy, the dramatic changes in the age profile of our population and the ecological tasks of our time are facts," he said.
"We Germans can't just go on doing what we always have. Anyone who tries to do this is gambling away our future."
Kohl urged unions, employers and politicians to work together to secure economic recovery, especially in the interests of the four million Germans who are out of work.
And he made clear that the scope of the welfare system would continue to be narrowed.

"Payments must benefit the truly needy," he said. "A glance over the border shows that all our important neighbours are being forced to go down a comparable path, for example France, the Netherlands and Sweden."

But Kohl made no direct mention of Economic and Monetary Union (EMU), his flagship project which has forced many of the austerity measures upon Germany and which will stand or fall based on members' economic performance in 1997.

While Kohl insists that a single currency is a vital step towards political union within the European Union, and that the "euro" will be every bit as strong a currency as the mark, surveys show most ordinary Germans do not share his confidence.
A poll by the INRA institute published on Monday found 54 percent of Germans surveyed felt the euro would bring them disadvantages while only 30 percent saw benefits.
